text_blocks.snippet: For the treatment of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), adenosine is generally considered the first-line medication, especially when atrioventricular (AV) node involvement is suspected. If adenosine is ineffective or contraindicated, calcium channel blockers like verapamil or diltiazem, or beta-blockers can be used. In hemodynamically unstable patients, synchronized cardioversion is the preferred approach.
snippet_highlighted_words: adenosine is generally considered the first-line medication

list.title: Adenosine:
list.snippet: This drug slows down electrical conduction through the AV node, effectively terminating many SVT episodes. It has a short half-life, making it a good choice for acute management.

list.title: Calcium Channel Blockers:
list.snippet: These medications, like verapamil and diltiazem, also work by blocking calcium channels, which can interrupt the electrical pathways involved in SVT. They are particularly useful when adenosine is not effective or is contraindicated.

list.title: Beta-Blockers:
list.snippet: Drugs like metoprolol, atenolol, or esmolol can also be used to slow the heart rate and manage SVT. They are often considered for long-term management.

list.title: Cardioversion:
list.snippet: For patients with unstable SVT (e.g., low blood pressure, chest pain, shortness of breath), immediate synchronized cardioversion is the appropriate treatment. This involves delivering a controlled electrical shock to restore a normal heart rhythm.

list.title: Other Options:
list.snippet: In specific situations, other medications like procainamide or amiodarone may be considered, especially if the SVT is associated with certain conditions like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

list.title: Long-term Management:
list.snippet: Besides medication, long-term management of SVT may involve catheter ablation, a procedure that destroys the abnormal electrical pathways in the heart.

text_blocks.snippet: Medications for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) include those used to terminate an acute episode and those used to prevent future episodes. Adenosine, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers are commonly used for acute episodes, while beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and antiarrhythmic drugs may be used for prevention.
snippet_highlighted_words: Adenosine, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers

list.title: Adenosine:
list.snippet: A first-line medication for acute SVT, especially when atrioventricular (AV) node involvement is suspected. It works by temporarily blocking the AV node and can help diagnose and treat certain types of SVT.

list.title: Beta-blockers:
list.snippet: Medications like metoprolol and esmolol can be used to slow the heart rate and terminate SVT. They work by blocking the effects of adrenaline on the heart.

list.title: Calcium Channel Blockers:
list.snippet: Diltiazem and verapamil are examples of calcium channel blockers that can be used to slow the heart rate and terminate SVT. They also help to control the ventricular rate in patients with atrial tachyarrhythmias.

list.title: Other options:
list.snippet: In some cases, other medications like amiodarone or procainamide may be used, especially if the SVT is resistant to other treatments or is associated with specific conditions like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

list.title: Synchronized Cardioversion:
list.snippet: This is a procedure where an electrical shock is delivered to the heart to restore a normal heart rhythm. It is typically used for patients with hemodynamically unstable SVT (where the patient's blood pressure and circulation are significantly affected).

list.title: Beta-blockers:
list.snippet: These are often used to prevent future episodes of SVT.

list.title: Calcium Channel Blockers:
list.snippet: Similar to their use in acute treatment, these can also be used to prevent future episodes.

list.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs:
list.snippet: Medications like amiodarone or sotalol may be prescribed to prevent SVT episodes.

list.title: Catheter Ablation:
list.snippet: This procedure is a more permanent solution for recurrent SVT. It involves using a catheter to deliver radiofrequency energy to selectively destroy the heart tissue that is causing the abnormal heart rhythm. It is a highly effective treatment for certain types of SVT.
